metadata.title: Profit, Loss, Discounts and Simple Interest
metadata.vcaa_description: Use mathematical modelling to solve practical problems involving rational numbers and percentages, including financial contexts.
metadata.target_mastery: Calculate profit, loss, and percentage profit/loss relative to cost price, evaluate successive discounts, and solve simple interest problems using I = Prt.

key_vocabulary.definition: The Cost Price is what a business pays to acquire or produce an item; the Selling Price is what the customer pays to buy it.
If $\text{SP} > \text{CP}$, the business makes a $\text{Profit} = \text{SP} - \text{CP}$. If $\text{SP} < \text{CP}$, it incurs a $\text{Loss} = \text{CP} - \text{SP}$.
Interest calculated as a fixed percentage $r$ of the initial principal $P$ for each time period $t$.

theory.title: Profit, Loss, and Percentage Profit/Loss on Cost Price
theory.explanation: Unless stated otherwise, percentage profit and percentage loss are always calculated as a percentage of the original Cost Price ($\text{CP}$).
theory.callout_rule: Whether calculating percentage profit or percentage loss, always divide the dollar profit or loss by the COST PRICE ($\text{CP}$), not the selling price.

theory.title: Successive Discounts
theory.explanation: When a store offers a second discount on an already discounted sale price (e.g., 'take a further $10\%$ off sale items'), the second percentage is applied to the intermediate sale price, not added to the first percentage. Multiply the individual discount multipliers together.
theory.callout_rule: A $20\%$ discount followed by a further $10\%$ discount is $0.80 \times 0.90 = 0.72$ ($28\%$ off in total), NOT $30\%$ off!

theory.title: Simple Interest and Total Amount ($I = Prt$ and $A = P + I$)
theory.explanation: When money is invested or borrowed at a simple interest rate of $r$ per annum (p.a.) for $t$ years on an initial principal $P$, the interest earned or charged is $I = Prt$ (where $r = \frac{R}{100}$ is written as a decimal or fraction). The total amount at the end of the term is $A = P + I$.
theory.formula_latex: I = P \times r \times t = \frac{P \times R \times t}{100}, \quad A = P + I
theory.callout_title: Match Time Units to the Interest Rate
theory.callout_rule: If the interest rate is given 'per annum' (per year) and the time is given in months, divide the number of months by $12$ to convert $t$ into years (e.g., $18\text{ months} = \frac{18}{12} = 1.5\text{ years}$).

worked_examples.title: Calculating Percentage Profit on Cost Price
worked_examples.problem: A Melbourne bicycle shop buys helmets for a cost price of $\$48$ each and sells them for $\$66$ each. Find (a) the profit per helmet and (b) the percentage profit on the cost price.

steps.thinking: Subtract the cost price ($\$48$) from the selling price ($\$66$) to find the dollar profit.
Divide the profit ($\$18$) by the cost price ($\$48$) and multiply by $100\%$.

now_you_try.problem: A bookshop in Carlton buys a textbook for $\$40$ and sells it for $\$54$. Find (a) the profit and (b) the percentage profit.
now_you_try.hint: Divide the profit by $\$40$ and multiply by $100\%$.

worked_examples.title: Simple Interest with Time in Months
worked_examples.problem: Noah invests $\$4000$ in an Australian term deposit paying $4.5\%$ per annum simple interest for $18\text{ months}$. Calculate (a) the simple interest earned and (b) the total value of the investment at the end of the $18\text{ months}$.

steps.thinking: Identify $P = 4000$, $r = \frac{4.5}{100} = 0.045$, and convert $18\text{ months}$ to years: $t = \frac{18}{12} = 1.5\text{ years}$.
Add the interest $I = \$270$ to the principal $P = \$4000$ to find the total final amount $A$.

now_you_try.problem: Chloe invests $\$6000$ at $5\%$ p.a. simple interest for $30\text{ months}$. Find (a) the interest earned and (b) the total final amount.

worked_examples.title: Rearranging the Simple Interest Formula to Find Principal or Time
worked_examples.problem: A small business in Dandenong borrows $\$12\,000$ at a simple interest rate of $6\%$ p.a. How many years did the loan run if the total simple interest paid was $\$2160$?

steps.thinking: Divide both sides by $720$ (the annual interest charge) to find $t$.

now_you_try.problem: An investor earns $\$960$ in simple interest over $4\text{ years}$ at a rate of $3\%$ p.a. What was the initial principal $P$ invested?

common_misconceptions.title: Forgetting to Convert Months into Years in $I = Prt$
common_misconceptions.misconception: Substituting $t = 9$ directly into $I = Prt$ for a $9$-month investment when $r$ is an annual ('per annum') interest rate.
common_misconceptions.correct_concept: Because 'per annum' means per year, $t$ must be expressed in years: $9\text{ months} = \frac{9}{12} = 0.75\text{ years}$. Substituting $t = 9$ overstates the interest by a factor of $12$.
common_misconceptions.counter_example: $9\text{ months}$ is less than $1\text{ year}$ ($\$80$ interest), so the interest must be less than $\$80$.

common_misconceptions.title: Adding Successive Discount Percentages Directly
common_misconceptions.misconception: Claiming that a $30\%$ discount followed by an extra $20\%$ off equals a $50\%$ discount.
common_misconceptions.correct_concept: The second discount of $20\%$ applies only to the remaining $70\%$ of the price ($0.20 \times 70\% = 14\%$), so the combined discount is $30\% + 14\% = 44\%$ (multiplier $0.70 \times 0.80 = 0.56$).
common_misconceptions.counter_example: If two successive $50\%$ discounts added to $100\%$, the item would be free instead of costing $0.5 \times 0.5 = 25\%$ of the original price!

fluency_and_understanding.question: A retailer buys a jacket for $\$80$ and sells it for $\$116$. Calculate the percentage profit.
A second-hand car bought for $\$15\,000$ is sold a year later for $\$12\,300$. Calculate the percentage loss.
Calculate the simple interest earned on $\$5000$ invested at $4\%$ p.a. for $3\text{ years}$.
Calculate the simple interest on a loan of $\$8400$ at $5.5\%$ p.a. for $8\text{ months}$.
A coat originally priced at $\$250$ is discounted by $20\%$, and then discounted by a further $15\%$ for VIP members. Find the final VIP price.
An investment of $\$7500$ grows to a total amount of $\$8850$ after $4\text{ years}$ of simple interest. Find the annual simple interest rate $R\%$.

problem_solving_and_modelling.question: A fruit vendor at the Queen Victoria Market buys $12$ crates of mangoes ($20$ mangoes per crate) for a total cost of $\$480$. Unfortunately, $15$ mangoes are bruised and cannot be sold. She sells the remaining mangoes for $\$3.00$ each. Calculate her overall percentage profit on the batch.

Two Melbourne department stores sell the same $\$400$ espresso machine. Store A offers a single flat discount of $35\%$. Store B offers '$25\%$ off, plus a further $12\%$ off the discounted price'. Which store offers the lower final price, and by how much?

Liam takes out a simple interest car loan of $\$18\,000$ at $6.5\%$ p.a. over $5\text{ years}$, to be repaid in $60$ equal monthly instalments covering both principal and interest. Calculate (a) the total amount to be repaid and (b) the monthly repayment.

reasoning_and_communication.question: Find the single percentage discount that is equivalent to two successive discounts of $20\%$ and $25\%$. Show why the order in which the two discounts are applied does not matter.
step_by_step_solution: By the commutative property of multiplication, $0.80 \times 0.75 = 0.75 \times 0.80 = 0.60$.
Since $60\%$ of the original price remains, the equivalent single discount is $100\% - 60\% = 40\%$.

reasoning_and_communication.question: How many years does it take for any positive principal $P$ to double in value under simple interest at $8\%$ per annum? Explain why the answer does not depend on the starting amount $P$.
step_by_step_solution: For the investment to double ($A = 2P$), the simple interest earned must equal the principal ($I = P$).
Substitute $I = P$ into $I = Prt$: $P = P \times 0.08 \times t$.
Dividing both sides by $P > 0$ cancels $P$ completely: $1 = 0.08t \implies t = \frac{1}{0.08} = 12.5\text{ years}$.

reasoning_and_communication.question: A shopkeeper marks up the cost price of an item by $40\%$, and then offers customers a $25\%$ discount off the marked price. Does the shopkeeper make a profit or a loss, and of what percentage on the cost price? Prove your answer algebraically.
step_by_step_solution: Let $C$ be the cost price. After a $40\%$ mark-up, the marked price is $1.40C$.
After a $25\%$ discount, the selling price is $0.75 \times 1.40C = 1.05C$.
Since $1.05C = C + 0.05C$, the shopkeeper makes a $5\%$ profit on the cost price.
